notes.summary: In para jumbles (sentence rearrangement) you get four to six sentences of a paragraph in mixed-up order and choose the option that puts them in a logical order. Sometimes the first and last sentences are fixed, and sometimes the jumbled pieces are parts of a single sentence. Every good paragraph has a clear opening, links between sentences (pronouns, repeated words, connectors, time order) and a natural ending. Find those links and you rarely need to test every option.

concepts.title: The fast method
concepts.body:
1. Find the opener: the sentence that makes sense on its own.
  2. Find one sure pair (two sentences that must sit together, e.g. a noun and the pronoun that refers to it).
  3. Eliminate options: keep only options that start with the opener and contain your pair.
  4. If two options remain, find the closing sentence or one more pair.
You almost never need to build the whole order yourself. Two clues usually leave one option.

concepts.title: Spotting the opening sentence
concepts.body:
A good opener introduces the topic and needs nothing before it.
Likely openerCannot be the opener
A general statement or definition: Tigers are the largest members of the cat family.Starts with a pronoun: They are found in…
Introduces a person or thing with a full name or a / an: A panther broke into a house.Starts with a connector: However, … / Therefore, … / Moreover, …
Sets time and place for a story: There lived a foolish king in a large kingdom.Refers back: This method… / Such habits… / The pump…
Gives the full form of a name: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted in 2015.Uses only the short form: The SDGs aim to…

concepts.title: Reference links: nouns, pronouns and articles
concepts.body:
• Noun before pronoun: Lata → she; the printing press → it; many people → they.
  • a before the: a water pump (first mention) → the pump (later).
  • Full form before short form: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) → the RBI.
  • Idea before this / that / such: People check their phones dozens of times an hour. → Such habits…
  • Repeated key word: a sentence ending with new land may be followed by one starting This land….
Check that the pronoun matches in number and gender: they cannot refer back to the farmer.

concepts.title: Connectors and what they need before them
concepts.body:
Connector at the startThe sentence before it must…
But, However, Yet, Neverthelesssay something the new sentence contrasts with
Therefore, Thus, So, As a result, Hencegive the cause of the result now stated
Moreover, Also, Besides, In addition, Furthermoremake a point of the same kind
For example, For instancemake a general claim that this example supports
In short, In conclusion, Finallycome near the end; this is often the last sentence
Despite this, Even sostate a problem or fact that is being overcome

concepts.title: Time order and process order
concepts.body:
Stories and processes follow time. Look for:
  • Sequence words: first, then, next, after that, later, finally, at last.
  • Time phrases: one day, the next morning, after a year, by noon, within an hour.
  • Dates: earlier years come first in a history paragraph.
  • Cause before effect: the machine kept failing → they replaced it.
  • Steps of a process: data was collected → analysed → conclusions drawn.
Example: Lata dreamed of a bicycle → she saved money every month → after a year she had enough → she rode it to work the next day.

concepts.title: General to specific
concepts.body:
Most essay-type paragraphs move from a general statement to details and examples, and end with a result, solution or opinion.
  1. General idea or problem
  2. Explanation or cause
  3. Example or details
  4. Result, solution or conclusion
Example: Mangroves grow on tropical coasts (general) → their roots break waves (benefit 1) → the roots also trap mud (benefit 2, linked by also) → moreover they shelter fish (benefit 3) → despite this, they are being cleared (problem) → protecting them is urgent (conclusion).

concepts.title: First and last sentences given
concepts.body:
When S1 and S6 are fixed:
  • The sentence right after S1 usually continues S1's subject or picks up its last idea.
  • The sentence right before S6 must lead into S6. If S6 starts with a pronoun or connector, its partner is just before it.
  • Work from both ends inward; the middle is then easy.

concepts.title: Parts of one sentence
concepts.body:
Here the pieces are phrases, not full sentences. Rebuild the grammar:
  1. Find the subject (often the piece with a capital letter or a noun phrase like one must).
  2. Attach the verb and its object.
  3. Add phrases of purpose, time or place (for a good body, in the evening).
  4. Clauses with but, which, because come after the idea they join.
Example: P: for a / Q: exercise daily / R: one must / S: good body → RQPS: One must exercise daily for a good body.

concepts.title: Mandatory pairs: a checklist
concepts.body:
• Noun → pronoun (she, it, they, this)
  • a + noun → the + same noun
  • Full name → short form or acronym
  • Question → answer
  • Claim → For example
  • Problem → As a result / Therefore
  • Statement → However / But (contrast)
  • Direct speech → the reply to it (in stories)
Finding even one of these pairs usually rules out two options.

varieties.name: Find the opening sentence
varieties.how: Choose the sentence that introduces the topic and makes sense alone: no starting pronoun, no connector, no this/such/the pointing back. Keep only options that begin with it.

example.q: A. They are found in forests across Asia. B. Tigers are the largest members of the cat family. C. However, their numbers have fallen sharply. D. Conservation projects have helped some populations recover. Options: ABCD / BACD / BCAD / CBAD
steps: A starts with They, C with However; neither can open.
B introduces tigers in general, so it opens. Only BACD and BCAD remain.
They in A refers to tigers, so A follows B. C contrasts with that, and D gives the recovery.

varieties.name: Pronoun and reference links
varieties.how: Match each pronoun, this/such, the X or short form to the sentence that first names it. Those two sentences sit together, noun first.

example.q: P: This made copying books by hand far less common. Q: The printing press was developed in Europe in the fifteenth century. R: As a result, more people learned to read. S: It allowed books to be produced quickly and cheaply. Options: QPSR / SQPR / QSPR / QSRP
steps: Q names the printing press, so it opens.
S's It refers to the press, so QS.
P's This refers to quick, cheap books in S, so QSP.

varieties.name: Connectors and time order
varieties.how: Use time words (then, after a year, finally) and connectors (but, therefore, as a result) to decide what must come before what.

example.q: P: But the machine kept failing in the rainy season. Q: The village bought a water pump to irrigate its fields. R: The villagers finally replaced it with a solar-powered model. S: For a few months, the pump worked well. Options: QSPR / QPSR / SQPR / QRSP
steps: Q introduces a water pump; it opens.
S (for a few months… worked well) comes before the contrast in P (But… kept failing).

varieties.name: First and last sentences given
varieties.how: Link the first middle sentence to S1 and the last middle sentence to S6, then fill the gap using pronouns and time order.

example.q: 1: The farmer woke up before sunrise. P: Then he led the bullocks to the field. Q: He fed his cattle and drank a glass of milk. R: By noon, half the field had been ploughed. S: There he began ploughing the dry soil. 6: He rested under a neem tree for lunch. Options: QSPR / QPSR / PQSR / QPRS
steps: After waking, he does his morning work at home: Q.
Then he goes to the field: P.
By noon leads into lunch in 6: R.

varieties.name: Parts of one sentence
varieties.how: Find the subject, join the verb and object to it, then add phrases of purpose, time or place at the end.

example.q: P: for a Q: exercise daily R: one must S: good body. Arrange to form a meaningful sentence. Options: PRQS / PRSQ / RQPS / PQRS

tips: Find the opener first; it alone often removes two options.
A sentence that starts with a pronoun or a connector is almost never the opener.
Look for one mandatory pair and check which options keep it together.
Full names and a + noun come before short forms and the + noun.
Words like finally, in short, thus usually mark the last sentence.
In stories, follow time: one day → then → later → finally.
Read your chosen order once from start to end; it should flow without jumps.
traps: Choosing a sentence with This or It as the opener because it sounds general.
A pronoun that looks like a link but does not match in number (they after the farmer).
Two options that differ only in the last two sentences: check the closing sentence carefully.
Putting an example (For instance…) before the claim it supports.
In sentence-part questions, joining phrases that sound fine but leave the sentence without a main verb.

questions.q:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful paragraph.
P: She saved a little money from her salary every month.
Q: Lata had always dreamed of owning a bicycle.
R: After a year, she finally had enough to buy one.
S: She rode it proudly to work the very next day.
questions.solution: Q introduces Lata and her dream (opener). P tells how she saved; R says after a year she had enough; S describes riding it. QPRS.

questions.q:
The first and last sentences are given. Rearrange P, Q, R, S.
1: The farmer woke up before sunrise.
P: Then he led the bullocks to the field.
Q: He fed his cattle and drank a glass of milk.
R: By noon, half the field had been ploughed.
S: There he began ploughing the dry soil.
6: He rested under a neem tree for lunch.
questions.solution: After waking, he feeds the cattle (Q), then leads bullocks to the field (P). There in S refers to the field → P before S. R (by noon) leads into lunch. QPSR.

questions.q:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful paragraph.
P: This made the old method of copying books by hand far less common.
Q: The printing press was developed in Europe in the fifteenth century.
R: As a result, more people learned to read.
S: It allowed books to be produced quickly and cheaply.
questions.solution: Q names the printing press (opener). S's It refers to the press. P's This refers to cheap production. R's As a result gives the final effect. QSPR.

questions.q:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful paragraph.
P: But the machine kept failing in the rainy season.
Q: The village bought a water pump to irrigate its fields.
R: The villagers finally replaced it with a solar-powered model.
S: For a few months, the pump worked well.
questions.solution: Q introduces the pump. S: it worked well at first. P: But contrasts with that success. R: finally replaced it. QSPR.

questions.q:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful paragraph.
P: Such habits, repeated daily, slowly change the brain's reward system.
Q: Many people check their phones dozens of times an hour.
R: Breaking the cycle therefore needs more than willpower; it needs a change of environment.
S: Each notification gives a small burst of pleasure that makes them check again.
questions.solution: Q states the general fact (opener). S explains why (them = many people). P's Such habits sums up Q and S. R's therefore draws the conclusion. QSPR.

questions.q:
The first and last sentences are given. Rearrange P, Q, R, S.
1: Mangroves grow along tropical coastlines where salt water meets land.
P: These roots also trap mud, slowly building new land.
Q: Their tangled roots break the force of waves during storms.
R: Despite these benefits, large areas have been cleared for fish farms.
S: Moreover, they shelter young fish and crabs.
6: Protecting the remaining forests is now an urgent task.
questions.solution: Q mentions tangled roots; P's These roots also continues it → QP. S's Moreover adds another benefit. R's Despite these benefits turns to the problem and leads to sentence 6. QPSR.

flashcards.front: Signs a sentence is NOT the opener
flashcards.back: Starts with a pronoun (he, it, this), or a connector (however, therefore, also, moreover).

flashcards.front: 'a X' vs 'the X' in para jumbles
flashcards.back: The sentence introducing 'a X' comes before the one mentioning 'the X'.
Find the opener + one mandatory pair, then eliminate options.
